purpose: Nitazoxanide is used to treat diarrhea caused by tiny parasites called Cryptosporidium and Giardia that can get into your digestive system, usually from contaminated water or food. It helps clear these infections so your gut can get back to normal. Your doctor may sometimes use it for other infections as well.
how_it_works: Nitazoxanide works by blocking a special energy-making process that parasites and some viruses need to survive. Think of it like cutting off the fuel supply to the bug causing your infection. Without that energy source, the parasites cannot live or multiply, and your body can clear them out.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, and vomiting. You may also notice that your urine turns a yellowish or pale green color — this is harmless and normal while taking this medicine. Most side effects are mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Let your doctor know about all other medicines you take, since nitazoxanide can interact with some drugs. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or think you might be pregnant, check with your doctor before taking this medication. Seek medical help right away if you develop a severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing.
typical_dosing: For adults and children 12 and older, the usual dose is 500 mg (one tablet or 25 mL of liquid) taken twice a day with food for 3 days. For children ages 4 to 11, the dose is usually 200 mg (10 mL of liquid) twice a day with food for 3 days. Children ages 1 to 3 typically take 100 mg (5 mL) twice a day with food for 3 days. Always take it with a meal to help it work better and reduce stomach upset.
